stimulus.text:
J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer, Letter III, “What Is an American?”, 1782:

“What then is the American, this new man? He is either an European, or the descendant of an European, hence that strange mixture of blood, which you will find in no other country. I could point out to you a family whose grandfather was an Englishman, whose wife was Dutch, whose son married a French woman, and whose present four sons have now four wives of different nations. He is an American, who leaving behind him all his ancient prejudices and manners, receives new ones from the new mode of life he has embraced, the new government he obeys, and the new rank he holds. ... Here individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men, whose labours and posterity will one day cause great changes in the world. ... The American is a new man, who acts upon new principles; he must therefore entertain new ideas, and form new opinions.”
stimulus.source_note: J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, Letters from an American Farmer (1782), Letter III. Public domain.

stem: According to Crèvecœur, what makes the American a “new man”?

options.text: He is descended from the oldest families of Europe.
options.misconception: The passage says the American leaves old prejudices behind, not that he comes from old families.

options.text: He is formed by many European peoples blending into one people with new principles.
He keeps the customs and ranks of the country his parents left.
options.misconception: The passage says he leaves behind his ancient prejudices and manners.

options.text: He is born in America to parents who were also born in America.
options.misconception: Background: Crèvecœur describes the American as a European or the descendant of a European, not as native-born for generations.

rationales.B: The passage says people of all nations are melted into a new race of men, and the new man acts on new principles.
rationales.A: The passage gives no weight to old families; it stresses new principles and a new mode of life.
rationales.C: Crèvecœur says the American leaves behind his ancient prejudices and manners.
rationales.D: The passage calls the American a European or the descendant of a European, so birth in America for generations is not the point.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men.
2. It adds that the American leaves behind his ancient prejudices and manners.
3. Background: Crèvecœur wrote in 1782, just as the new nation was taking shape after independence.
4. So the “new man” is new because many peoples blend and live by new principles, not because of one ancestry.
Remember: when a writer calls a people new, look for what changed in their lives, not only where they came from.
